report:
**Conclusion:** Current evidence does not support that coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) meaningfully improves movement symptoms in Parkinson’s disease (PD). Your view (“no”) aligns with the best available clinical trial data.

**Evidence:**
- An early randomized, double-blind pilot trial (Shults et al., 2002) reported a possible slowing of functional decline on the Unified Parkinson’s Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS) at 1,200 mg/day, but the study was small and not designed to confirm efficacy.
- A large multicenter phase III trial by the Parkinson Study Group (QE3) was stopped early for futility because interim analysis showed CoQ10 was unlikely to produce a clinically meaningful benefit over placebo on total UPDRS or motor outcomes.
- A systematic review of CoQ10 and parkinsonian syndromes concluded that, despite biological plausibility (antioxidant and mitochondrial support), clinical trial evidence does not demonstrate significant improvement in motor symptoms.
- A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials found no statistically significant benefit of CoQ10 on UPDRS motor scores compared with placebo, and noted heterogeneity and limited trial quality.

Overall, while CoQ10 is generally safe and biologically plausible, well-powered randomized trials and meta-analyses have not shown a reliable improvement in Parkinson’s movement disorders.

- https://www.mdpi.com/2075-4426/12/6/975
- https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9225264/
- https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10072-016-2757-9
